method: Rebuild from primary text. Cal. Lab. Code §230 was fetched in full from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov; the voting provisions were fetched as Elections Code Division 14, Chapter 1 (§§14000-14004), which is where they actually live — the clause cited them to the Labor Code. 29 C.F.R. §541.602 was fetched from the eCFR to check the exempt-salary sentence, which is federal and was also cited to the Labor Code. The construing case was located through CourtListener. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Cal. Elec. Code Division 14 Chapter 1 full text (leginfo)
"Labor Code section 230" jury duty discharge discriminate reasonable notice

assertions.text: §230(a) forbids discharge or discrimination for taking time off to serve on an inquest or trial jury, if the employee gives reasonable notice before taking the time off
assertions.note: §230(a), verbatim. The notice condition is part of the protection, not a separate courtesy: an employee who does not give it is outside the subdivision. The previous body stated the leave unconditionally.

assertions.text: §230(b) forbids discharge, discrimination or retaliation for taking time off to appear in court under a subpoena or other court order as a witness
assertions.note: §230(b), verbatim. Note that unlike (a) it carries no notice condition.

assertions.text: §230 does not require the employer to pay for jury service and does not reach time off taken when the employee is not serving
assertions.note: People v. Hing Kwee, quoted below. This is the construction that changes what the section is: not a leave entitlement but an anti-discrimination rule. The previous body opened with 'Provide unpaid leave for jury service', which reads as a duty to grant leave that §230 does not impose in those terms.

assertions.text: the employee may use accrued vacation, personal leave or compensatory time off, and a collective bargaining agreement cannot diminish the entitlement
assertions.note: §230(i), verbatim. Absent from the previous body.

assertions.text: an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which they perform any work, without regard to days or hours, subject to the permitted deductions
assertions.note: 29 C.F.R. §541.602(a)(1), verbatim: 'Subject to the exceptions provided in paragraph (b) of this section, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work without regard to the number of days or hours worked.' The previous body said 'generally must be paid' and cited the Labor Code, which does not contain this rule. §541.602(b)(1) permits a deduction for a full-day personal absence other than sickness or disability, which is exactly the situation a jury-service week can present.

assertions.text: a voter without sufficient time outside working hours may take enough working time to vote at a statewide election, of which no more than two hours is without loss of pay
assertions.note: Elec. Code §14000(a)-(b). The two hours is the paid ceiling, not the ceiling on time off; the previous body's 'up to two (2) hours of paid time off to vote' collapses the two.

assertions.text: the time is taken at the beginning or end of the shift unless otherwise mutually agreed
assertions.note: Elec. Code §14000(b), and the section adds the criterion: whichever 'allows the most free time for voting and the least time off from the regular working shift'.

assertions.text: an employee who knows on the third working day before the election that time off will be needed must give at least two working days' notice
assertions.note: Elec. Code §14000(c). The previous body stated the entitlement and omitted the precondition, which its own defect list had already identified.

assertions.text: a notice setting out §14000 must be posted not less than 10 days before every statewide election
an employer shall not require or request that an employee bring a vote-by-mail ballot to work or vote it at work
assertions.note: Elec. Code §14004, added by Stats. 2019, Ch. 223. Absent from the previous body, and it is the provision most likely to be violated inadvertently by a well-meaning employer running a 'vote at lunch' event; §14004(b) preserves encouragement to vote.

priorDefects: wrong-citation: 'Cal. Lab. Code §§230, 14350-14353'. There is no Labor Code §14350. Voting leave is Elections Code §§14000-14004. Every voting assertion in the clause rested on a citation to the wrong code.
wrong-citation: the exempt-salary sentence is 29 C.F.R. §541.602(a)(1), a federal regulation. It was cited to the California Labor Code.

contradicted in substance: 'Provide unpaid leave for jury service and for appearing as a witness under subpoena' states §230 as a leave mandate. Hing Kwee: 'Nothing in Labor Code section 230 mandates that employees be paid for time they take off to serve on a jury; the provision states only that employers shall not discriminate.'
omitted: the two-working-days notice condition in Elec. Code §14000(c).
omitted: that the two-hour figure is the paid ceiling, not the ceiling on time off.
omitted: §230(i), the right to use accrued leave.

unsupported (rationale): 'discipline for jury service is a misdemeanor'. §230(g)(3) makes it a misdemeanor to WILFULLY REFUSE to rehire, promote or restore an employee already determined eligible by a grievance procedure or hearing. Hing Kwee describes the same mechanism. Discipline is not itself the misdemeanor.
gaps: Labor Code §230(c)-(f) protects a victim of crime or abuse and requires reasonable accommodation for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Those subdivisions were read and are not carried, because the corpus has a separate hb_ca_victim_leave clause. That clause was not examined here and may not state them correctly.
No remedy for a voting-leave violation was found in the text of Elec. Code §§14000-14004 and none was researched. The clause states duties with no consequence attached.
Whether an employer may require documentation of jury service was not researched and is not addressed.

29 C.F.R. §541.602(b) has eight exception categories. Only the full-day personal absence in (b)(1) is named in the clause. An employer relying on another of them gets no help here, and California imposes its own limits on salary deductions that were not read — the California Code of Regulations publisher, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy.

judicialQuotations.case: People v. Hing Kwee (Cal. Ct. App. 1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1
judicialQuotations.quote: Nothing in Labor Code section 230 mandates that employees be paid for time they take off to serve on a jury; the provision states only that employers shall not discriminate against employees "for taking time off to serve as required by law on [a] . . . trial jury."

judicialQuotations.case: People v. Hing Kwee (Cal. Ct. App. 1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1
judicialQuotations.quote: Labor Code section 230 does not purport to apply to time taken off when not serving on a jury. The court had no jurisdiction under Labor Code section 230 to require the employer (1) to compensate a juror/employee, or (2) to give time off ... when he was not serving on a trial jury.

judicialQuotations.case: People v. Hing Kwee (Cal. Ct. App. 1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1
judicialQuotations.quote: The Legislature has not seen fit to require employers to compensate employees for time taken off from work to serve on a jury; it is not within the province of the court to impose additional burdens not ...

currencyCaveat: Hing Kwee is from 1995 and quotes §230 as it then read, in its 'No employer shall' form and with fewer subdivisions; §230 has since been amended repeatedly and now runs to subdivision (j). The two propositions relied on here — that §230 does not require pay and does not reach non-service time — turn on the phrase 'for taking time off to serve', which is unchanged in the current §230(a). The third quotation is cut off in the source excerpt at 'not ...' and should be re-read in full before it is quoted anywhere a reader will rely on it.
